parrafos: Impressionism was a 19th-century art movement characterised by visible brush strokes, open composition, emphasis on accurate depiction of light in its changing qualities (often accentuating the effects of the passage of time), ordinary subject matter, unusual visual angles, and inclusion of movement as a crucial element of human perception and experience. Impressionism originated with a group of Paris-based artists whose independent exhibitions brought them to prominence during the 1870s and 1880s.

The Impressionists faced harsh opposition from the conventional art community in France. The name of the style derives from the title of a Claude Monet work, Impression, Sunrise, which provoked the critic Louis Leroy to coin the term in a satirical 1874 review of the First Impressionist Exhibition published in the Parisian newspaper Le Charivari. The development of Impressionism in the visual arts was soon followed by analogous styles in other media that became known as Impressionist music and Impressionist literature.

Radicals in their time, the early Impressionists violated the rules of academic painting. They constructed their pictures from freely brushed colours that took precedence over lines and contours, following the example of painters such as Eugène Delacroix and J. M. W. Turner. They also painted realistic scenes of everyday life in natural settings, often outdoors, attempting to capture a moment as experienced.

Previously, paintings were accomplished in studio, whether landscape art, still life or portrait, with an emphasis on verisimilitude. The Impressionists found that they could capture the momentary and transient effects of sunlight by painting outdoors or en plein air. They portrayed overall visual effects instead of details, and used short "broken" brush strokes of mixed and pure unmixed colour—not blended smoothly or shaded, as was customary—to achieve an effect of intense colour vibration.

Impressionism emerged in France at the same time that a number of other painters, including the Italian artists known as the Macchiaioli, and Winslow Homer in the United States, were also exploring plein-air painting. The Impressionists, however, developed new techniques specific to the style. Encompassing what its adherents argued was a different way of seeing, it is an art of immediacy and movement, of candid poses and compositions, of the play of light expressed in a bright and varied use of colour. In 1876, the poet and critic Stéphane Mallarmé said of the new style: "The represented subject, being composed of a harmony of reflected and ever-changing lights, cannot be supposed always to look the same but palpitates with movement, light, and life".

The public, at first hostile, gradually came to believe that the Impressionists had captured a fresh and original vision, even if the art critics and art establishment disapproved of the new style. By recreating the sensation in the eye that views the subject, rather than delineating the details of the subject, and by creating a welter of techniques and forms, Impressionism is a precursor of various painting styles, including Post-Impressionism, Fauvism, and Cubism.

In the middle of the 19th century—a time of rapid industrialisation and unsettling social change in France, as Emperor Napoleon III rebuilt Paris and waged war—the Académie des Beaux-Arts dominated French art. The Académie was the preserver of traditional French painting standards of content and style. Historical subjects, religious themes, and portraits were valued; landscape and still life were not. The Académie preferred carefully finished images that looked realistic when examined closely. Paintings in this style were made up of precise brush strokes carefully blended to hide the artist's hand in the work. Colour was restrained and often toned down further by the application of a thick golden varnish.

The Académie had an annual, juried art show, the Salon de Paris, and artists whose work was displayed in the show won prizes, garnered commissions, and enhanced their prestige. The standards of the juries represented the values of the Académie, represented by the works of such artists as Jean-Léon Gérôme and Alexandre Cabanel. Using an eclectic mix of techniques and formulas established in Western painting since the Renaissance, such as linear perspective and figure types derived from Classical Greek art, these artists produced escapist visions of a reassuringly ordered world. By the 1850s, some artists, notably the Realist painter Gustave Courbet, had gained public attention and critical censure by depicting contemporary realities without the idealisation demanded by the Académie.

In the early 1860s, four young painters—Claude Monet, Pierre-Auguste Renoir, Alfred Sisley, and Frédéric Bazille—met while studying under the academic artist Charles Gleyre. They discovered that they shared an interest in painting landscape and contemporary life rather than historical or mythological scenes. Following a practice—pioneered by artists such as the Englishman John Constable— that had become increasingly popular by mid-century, they often ventured into the countryside together to paint in the open air. Their purpose was not to make sketches to be developed into carefully finished works in the studio, as was the usual custom, but to complete their paintings out-of-doors.

By painting in sunlight directly from nature, and making bold use of the vivid synthetic pigments that had become available since the beginning of the century, they began to develop a lighter and brighter manner of painting that extended further the Realism of Courbet and the Barbizon school. A favourite meeting place for the artists was the Café Guerbois on Avenue de Clichy in Paris, where the discussions were often led by Édouard Manet, whom the younger artists greatly admired. They were soon joined by Camille Pissarro, Paul Cézanne, and Armand Guillaumin.

During the 1860s, the Salon jury routinely rejected about half of the works submitted by Monet and his friends in favour of works by artists faithful to the approved style. In 1863, the Salon jury rejected Manet's Le déjeuner sur l'herbe, 'The Luncheon on the Grass', primarily because it depicted a nude woman with two clothed men at a picnic. While the Salon jury routinely accepted nudes in historical and allegorical paintings, they condemned Manet for placing a realistic nude in a contemporary setting. The jury's severely worded rejection of Manet's painting appalled his admirers, and the unusually large number of rejected works that year perturbed many French artists.

After Emperor Napoleon III saw the rejected works of 1863, he decreed that the public be allowed to judge the work themselves, and the French: Salon des Refusés, lit. 'Salon of the Refused' was organised. While many viewers came only to laugh, the Salon des Refusés drew attention to the existence of a new tendency in art and attracted more visitors than the regular Salon.

Artists' petitions requesting a new Salon des Refusés in 1867, and again in 1872, were denied. In December 1873, Monet, Renoir, Pissarro, Sisley, Cézanne, Berthe Morisot, Edgar Degas and several other artists founded the Société anonyme des artistes peintres, sculpteurs, graveurs, etc., 'Anonymous Society of painters, sculptors, engravers, etc.' to exhibit their artworks independently. Members of the association were expected to forswear participation in the Salon. The organisers invited a number of other progressive artists to join them in their inaugural exhibition, including the older Eugène Boudin, whose example had first persuaded Monet to adopt plein air painting years before. Another painter who greatly influenced Monet and his friends, Johan Jongkind, declined to participate, as did Édouard Manet. In total, thirty artists participated in their first exhibition, held in April 1874 at the studio of the photographer Nadar.

The critical response was mixed. Monet and Cézanne received the harshest attacks. Critic and humorist Louis Leroy wrote a scathing review in the newspaper Le Charivari in which, making wordplay with the title of Claude Monet's Impression, Sunrise, he gave the artists the name by which they became known. Derisively titling his article "The Exhibition of the Impressionists", Leroy declared that Monet's painting was at most, a sketch, and could hardly be termed a finished work.

"Impression—I was certain of it. I was just telling myself that, since I was impressed, there had to be some impression in it... and what freedom, what ease of workmanship! Wallpaper in its embryonic state is more finished than that seascape."

The term Impressionist quickly gained favour with the public. It was also accepted by the artists themselves, even though they were a diverse group in style and temperament, unified primarily by their spirit of independence and rebellion. They exhibited together regardless of shifting membership eight times between 1874 and 1886. The Impressionists' style, with its loose, spontaneous brushstrokes, would soon become synonymous with modern life. Monet, Sisley, Morisot, and Pissarro may be considered the "purest" Impressionists, in their consistent pursuit of an art of spontaneity, sunlight, and colour. Degas rejected much of this, as he believed in the primacy of drawing over colour and belittled the practice of painting outdoors. Renoir turned away from Impressionism for a time during the 1880s, and never entirely regained his commitment to its ideas. Édouard Manet, although regarded by the Impressionists as their leader, never abandoned his liberal use of black as a colour (while Impressionists avoided its use and preferred to obtain darker colours by mixing), and never participated in the Impressionist exhibitions. He continued to submit his works to the Salon, where his painting Spanish Singer had won a 2nd class medal in 1861, and he urged the others to do likewise, arguing that "the Salon is the real field of battle" where a reputation could be made.

The artists of the core group gradually reduced. Bazille died in the Franco-Prussian War in 1870. Defections occurred as Cézanne, followed later by Renoir, Sisley, and Monet, abstained from the group exhibitions so they could submit their works to the Salon. Disagreements arose from issues such as Guillaumin's membership in the group, championed by Pissarro and Cézanne against opposition from Monet and Degas, who thought him unworthy. Degas invited Mary Cassatt to display her work in the 1879 exhibition, but also insisted on the inclusion of Jean-François Raffaëlli, Ludovic Lepic, and other realists who did not represent Impressionist practices, causing Monet in 1880 to accuse the Impressionists of "opening doors to first-come daubers".
resumen_es: The origins, techniques and early years of Impressionism: its break with academic painting and the Paris Salon, the independent exhibitions held from 1874 onwards, and the internal tensions within the group.

ideas_clave.idea: Impressionism was a nineteenth-century movement, launched by a group of Parisian painters in the 1870s and 1880s, that focused on changing light, everyday subjects and movement, rendered with visible brushwork.

Despite fierce resistance from the French art establishment, the movement took its name from a mocking 1874 review of Monet's Impression, Sunrise, and it later inspired parallel trends in music and literature.

Breaking with academic rules, the painters gave colour priority over line, left the studio to work outdoors and used short, unblended strokes to capture the fleeting effects of light, developing techniques of their own even though others also painted outdoors.
Although critics remained hostile, the public slowly accepted this new way of seeing, which paved the way for Post-Impressionism, Fauvism and Cubism.

At the time, the Académie des Beaux-Arts imposed polished, idealised historical and religious painting, and success depended on its annual Salon, although realists such as Courbet had begun to challenge these conventions.
In the early 1860s Monet, Renoir, Sisley and Bazille began finishing their landscapes outdoors with bright synthetic pigments, meeting other painters around Manet at the Café Guerbois.

The Salon jury regularly turned down their work, and the scandal over Manet's Le déjeuner sur l'herbe in 1863 led Napoleon III to authorise a Salon des Refusés, which proved more popular than the official show.
After further requests were refused, the artists set up an independent society in 1873 and held their first exhibition, with thirty participants, in Nadar's studio in April 1874.
Reactions were mixed, and Louis Leroy's sarcastic article, which dismissed Monet's canvas as a mere sketch, gave the group its label.
The artists adopted the name and exhibited together eight times until 1886, although they differed widely in style, and Manet, their acknowledged leader, kept sending his work to the Salon.
The original group gradually broke up because of Bazille's death, defections to the Salon and quarrels over who should be admitted.

resumen_modelo: The text explains the origins and early development of Impressionism, a nineteenth-century movement born in Paris that sought to render the shifting effects of light, ordinary scenes and movement through visible brushwork. Rejecting academic conventions, its painters gave priority to colour over line, worked outdoors rather than in the studio and used short, unblended strokes to convey a fleeting moment; consequently, although they initially faced hostility, they gradually won over the public and paved the way for Post-Impressionism, Fauvism and Cubism. This break must be understood against the background of the Académie des Beaux-Arts, which favoured historical and religious subjects, polished finishes and subdued colour, and whose annual Salon was the main route to recognition, even though realists such as Courbet had already begun to depict contemporary life without idealisation. In the early 1860s, Monet, Renoir, Sisley and Bazille, who shared a taste for landscape and modern life, began painting in the open air with bright synthetic pigments and gathered around Manet. Since the Salon jury systematically rejected their work, most notoriously Manet's Le déjeuner sur l'herbe in 1863, Napoleon III authorised a Salon des Refusés, which drew large crowds. When further requests were turned down, the artists founded an independent society and held their first exhibition in 1874. Reviews were mixed, and a mocking article by Louis Leroy, playing on Monet's Impression, Sunrise, gave the group its name. The label was nevertheless adopted, and these painters, diverse yet united by a spirit of independence, exhibited together eight times until 1886, although Degas and Renoir distanced themselves from some of its principles. However, internal disputes, defections to the Salon and Bazille's death progressively weakened the core group, while Manet himself never took part.

preguntas.enunciado: Say whether the statement is true, false or not stated in the text.
preguntas.pregunta: The term “Impressionism” was coined by Claude Monet himself.
preguntas.cita: which provoked the critic Louis Leroy to coin the term in a satirical 1874 review
preguntas.explicacion: The term was coined by the critic Louis Leroy in a satirical review, based on the title of a painting by Monet. Monet only painted the work that gave rise to the name.

preguntas.enunciado: Answer in your own words (1–3 sentences).
preguntas.pregunta: In what sense were the early Impressionists “radicals in their time”?
respuestas: They broke the rules of academic painting: they built their pictures from freely applied colour rather than precise lines and contours, and they painted realistic scenes of everyday life outdoors, trying to capture a moment as it was experienced.
preguntas.cita: Radicals in their time, the early Impressionists violated the rules of academic painting.
preguntas.explicacion: The paragraph explains what the break consisted of: colour taking priority over line, and everyday scenes painted outdoors. A good answer should mention both.

preguntas.pregunta: How did the Impressionists apply colour to achieve an effect of intense vibration?
opciones: In short, broken strokes of mixed and pure colour
In thin washes covered with golden varnish
In precise lines that defined each contour
respuestas: In short, broken strokes of mixed and pure colour
preguntas.cita: used short "broken" brush strokes of mixed and pure unmixed colour—not blended smoothly or shaded, as was customary
preguntas.explicacion: The text talks about short, “broken” brush strokes of pure and mixed colour. Smooth blending and a golden varnish were typical of academic painting, and precise lines are exactly what they abandoned.

preguntas.enunciado: Find a word in paragraph 3 that means “the appearance of being real or true”.
preguntas.pregunta: Find a word meaning “the appearance of being true or real”.
preguntas.explicacion: “Verisimilitude” is the quality of seeming real; studio painting aimed above all at this effect.

preguntas.pregunta: According to the text, Impressionism was a precursor of which styles?
preguntas.cita: Impressionism is a precursor of various painting styles, including Post-Impressionism, Fauvism, and Cubism.
preguntas.explicacion: The text explicitly names these three styles. Realism and the Barbizon school are forerunners, not successors, and academic painting is what Impressionism rejected.

preguntas.enunciado: Say whether the statement is true, false or not stated in the text.
preguntas.pregunta: The Académie valued landscape and still life more highly than historical subjects.
preguntas.cita: Historical subjects, religious themes, and portraits were valued; landscape and still life were not.
preguntas.explicacion: It is the other way round: the Académie valued historical and religious subjects and portraits, and did not value landscape or still life.

preguntas.enunciado: Find a word in paragraph 7 that means “obtained, gathered” (of commissions).
preguntas.pregunta: Find a verb meaning “obtained, collected” (used with “commissions”).
preguntas.cita: won prizes, garnered commissions, and enhanced their prestige
preguntas.explicacion: “To garner” means to obtain or gather something, often support or recognition; here, commissions for works.

preguntas.pregunta: Where did Monet, Renoir, Sisley and Bazille meet in the early 1860s?
opciones: At the studio of the photographer Nadar
preguntas.cita: met while studying under the academic artist Charles Gleyre
preguntas.explicacion: They met as students of Gleyre. The Café Guerbois was later their meeting place, the Salon was the official exhibition, and Nadar’s studio hosted the 1874 exhibition.

preguntas.pregunta: The discussions at the Café Guerbois were often led by Édouard Manet.
preguntas.cita: where the discussions were often led by Édouard Manet, whom the younger artists greatly admired
preguntas.explicacion: The text says so in exactly these terms: Manet often led the discussions and the young painters admired him.

preguntas.pregunta: Why did the Salon jury condemn Manet's Le déjeuner sur l'herbe?
opciones: Because it placed a realistic nude in a contemporary setting
Because nudes were never accepted at the Salon
Because it depicted a historical scene
respuestas: Because it placed a realistic nude in a contemporary setting
preguntas.cita: they condemned Manet for placing a realistic nude in a contemporary setting
preguntas.explicacion: The problem was not the nude itself, which was accepted in historical or allegorical paintings, but placing it in a contemporary scene. Nothing is said about it being painted outdoors.

preguntas.cita: wrote a scathing review in the newspaper Le Charivari
preguntas.explicacion: “Scathing” describes fierce, contemptuous criticism; common collocation: “a scathing review/attack”.

preguntas.enunciado: Answer in your own words (1–3 sentences).
preguntas.pregunta: Why did Manet never take part in the Impressionist exhibitions, even though the group regarded him as its leader?
respuestas: Manet believed that a reputation could only be built at the official Salon, which he called the real battlefield, so he kept submitting his works there and urged the others to do the same; he also kept using black, unlike the Impressionists.
preguntas.cita: arguing that "the Salon is the real field of battle" where a reputation could be made
preguntas.explicacion: The main reason is strategic: Manet was still betting on the Salon, where he had already won a medal. The difference in the use of black is an additional feature.

preguntas.enunciado: Answer in your own words (1–3 sentences).
preguntas.pregunta: What factors weakened the core group of Impressionists?
respuestas: Bazille died in the Franco-Prussian War, several members such as Cézanne, Renoir, Sisley and Monet stopped exhibiting with the group to return to the Salon, and there were disputes over membership, for example about Guillaumin or the realists invited by Degas.
preguntas.cita: The artists of the core group gradually reduced.
preguntas.explicacion: The paragraph lists three causes: a death, defections to the Salon and disputes over who should be part of the group.
